title: Managing Stakeholder Expectations
titleEs: Gestionar las expectativas de las partes interesadas
summary: Give a stakeholder a date they can plan around without promising what you cannot keep: evidence in the Present Perfect Continuous (*we've been seeing fewer errors since the fix*), a graded forecast (*should*, *is likely to*, *is expected to*), a firm commitment and the risks that could move it.
canDo: Justify a forecast with a trend: *we've been seeing… since…, so…*
Grade how sure I am: *will* (firm), *should / is expected to* (probable), *is likely to / may* (possible), *it's too early to say* (no forecast).
Commit to a date and name the one I am aiming for, with the main risk.
Reduce *to* and *should* in *likely to* and *should be*, and say *at this stage* without an extra /e/.

focus.grammar: Present Perfect Continuous for the evidence behind a forecast · hedged predictions: should, is likely to, is expected to, may · firm vs tentative commitments: will vs should · it's too early to say whether · unless / provided that
focus.lexis: manage expectations, under-promise and over-deliver, a realistic timeline, build in a buffer, best-case / worst-case scenario, commit to (a date), a firm date / a tentative date, it's too early to say, a trade-off, no promises
focus.afh: weak forms: likely to /tə/, should be /ʃəd/ · linking and s-cluster in at this stage · sceNArio (four syllables, /s/) · comMIT to

warmup: Someone asks you when something will be ready and you are not sure. In your language, how do you answer without lying and without sounding weak? Which words do you use to soften the date?

scenario.title: I need a date the board can commit to
scenario.context: Helen leaves Ryan a voice message after a board meeting. She needs a firm go-live date and the risks to it, not a story.
scenario.speaker: helen
scenario.text: Hi Ryan, Helen here. I've just come out of the board meeting, and they{{'ve been asking}} me for a {{firm}} go-live date. I know you{{'ve been dealing with}} the supplier issue, but I need something I can {{commit to}}. {{Realistically}}, what's the earliest we can go live, and what would have to go wrong for that date to slip? Call me back when you can. Thanks.

dialogue.title: Deciding what to promise
dialogue.context: Ryan brings Helen's question to the team. They have to agree on a date they can keep.

lines.speaker: ryan

discovery.text: Since the fix, we{{'ve been seeing}} far fewer export errors, so the reporting module {{should be}} ready by June 6. If the supplier changes the format again, we{{'re likely to}} lose another week. {{At this stage}}, it's too early to say whether the search will be in the first release. discovery.tts: Since the fix, we've been seeing far fewer export errors, so the reporting module [should](/ʃəd/) be ready by June sixth. organizer.title: How firm is it?
organizer.prompt: Complete the table: how firm is each sentence (firm, likely, possible, unknown), and which words signal it?
rows: The module {{should be}} ready by June 6.
We{{'re likely to}} lose another week.
{{It's too early to say}} whether the search will be in the first release.
organizer.explain: *Commit to* and *will* are firm; *should* and *is expected to* are probable; *is likely to* and *may* are possible; *too early to say* makes no forecast at all.

questions.q: Alex says *we've been seeing fewer errors since the fix, so the module should be ready by June 6*. What is the evidence and what is the forecast? How sure is *should*: a promise, a probability or a wish?
questions.model: The evidence is the trend: *we've been seeing fewer errors since the fix*, an observation that started in the past and continues. The forecast is *should be ready by June 6*. *Should* here is a reasoned expectation: probable, based on evidence, but not a promise. A promise would be *will be ready*; a wish would be *hopefully it'll be ready*.
criteria: You separated the evidence (*have been seeing… since*) from the forecast (*should be ready*).
You said *should* expresses a probable expectation based on evidence, not a promise.
You contrasted it with a firm *will* (promise) or a weaker form (*hopefully*, *might*).

questions.q: List the hedging forms in the text and the dialogue: *should be*, *is likely to*, *is expected to*, *it's too early to say whether*, *at this stage*. Write the pattern of each (what comes after it) and put them in order from firmest to most open.

signals.label: too early to say whether + clause

questions.model: From firmest to most open: *will + verb* (firm) > *is expected to + verb* and *should + verb* (probable, based on evidence) > *is likely to + verb* and *may + verb* (possible) > *it's too early to say whether + clause* (no forecast). *At this stage* and *realistically* are adverbials that frame any of them as provisional. Patterns: *should be ready*, *is likely to lose*, *is expected to be delivered*, *too early to say whether the search will…*.
criteria: You listed the forms with what follows each (*should + verb*, *likely to + verb*, *too early to say whether + clause*).
You ordered them from firmest (*will*) to most open (*too early to say*).
You noted that *at this stage* / *realistically* mark the forecast as provisional.

questions.q: Ryan chooses to *commit to June 20 and aim for the 6th*. What does the board gain, what does the team gain, and what is the risk of promising June 6 directly? Why is *it's too early to say* better than silence about the search?
questions.model: The board gets a firm date it can plan around; the team gets a buffer and the chance to over-deliver. Promising June 6 directly sounds better today but turns one supplier change into a broken promise. Saying *it's too early to say whether the search will be in the first release* names an open risk early, so the client can plan for it; silence would make the same news a surprise later, which costs more trust than the risk itself.
criteria: You said the firm later date protects the team and gives the client something to plan with.
You said a direct promise of the early date risks becoming a broken promise.
You said naming an open risk early (*too early to say*) protects trust more than silence.

points: Give the evidence first with the Present Perfect Continuous (*we've been seeing fewer errors since the fix*), then the forecast.

Grade the forecast: *will* (firm) > *is expected to / should* (probable) > *is likely to / may* (possible) > *it's too early to say whether* (no forecast yet). *At this stage*, *realistically* and *unless* frame it as provisional.
Commit to the date you can keep and name the one you are aiming for: *we're committing to June 20 and aiming for the 6th*.
Name open risks early (*whether the search will be in the first release*): a surprise later costs more trust than a risk stated now.
formulas: have / has been + -ing + since / for (evidence) → should / is likely to / is expected to + verb (forecast)
best case + date · worst case + date · unless / provided that + clause
it's too early to say whether + clause · at this stage, … · realistically, …
rule.note: Spanish often promises with the future (*estará listo el 6*) and softens it with the tone of voice. English softens with the verb: *should be ready*, *is likely to*, *we expect to*. A bare *will* is a commitment.

phonetics.intro: Las previsiones se construyen con palabras funcionales que casi desaparecen: *likely to* es «LÁIK-li-ta» y *should be*, «shad-bi». El hispanohablante tiende a darles vocal plena y a añadir una /e/ delante de *stage*. Aquí trabajamos esas formas débiles, el enlace de *at this stage* y los acentos de *scenario* y *commit*.

items.meaning: probably going to; used before a verb to make a possible prediction

alerts.text: *To* delante de consonante es /tə/, «ta», con schwa. Nunca «tu» con vocal plena: eso es *too* o *two*.
El acento está en LAIK; *to* no lleva ninguno. «LÁIK-li-ta», tres sílabas cuesta abajo.
*Likely to lose*: un solo bloque, «LÁIK-li-ta-LUUZ», sin pausa delante de *to*.

example.speaker: oliver
example.text: If the format changes again, we're likely to lose another week.
example.tts: If the format changes again, we're likely [to](/tə/) lose another week.

items.meaning: will probably be, based on what we know

alerts.text: En *it should be ready*, *should* se reduce a /ʃəd/, «shad». La vocal plena /ʊ/ solo aparece al final (*Yes, we should*) o al negar (*shouldn't*).
La l de *should* es muda: «shad», nunca «shuld».
*Be* es /bi/, breve y sin énfasis: «shad-bi», dos sílabas rápidas antes de la palabra que importa (*ready*).

example.speaker: alex
example.text: The module should be ready by the sixth.
example.tts: The module [should](/ʃəd/) be ready by the sixth.

items.meaning: at this point in the process; now, with the information we have

alerts.text: *Stage* empieza con /st/, sin e de apoyo: «at-dhis-STÉIDY», nunca «es-TÉIDY».
*At* y *this* se funden: «a(t)-dhis», la t casi no explota; luego la s de *this* se pega a la de *stage*.
*-ge* final es /dʒ/, «dy», con voz: «steidy». No «steish» ni «steich».

example.speaker: priya
example.text: At this stage it's too early to say whether the search will be in the first release.

items.meaning: a possible sequence of events; best-case / worst-case scenario

alerts.text: Acento en la segunda sílaba y cuatro sílabas: «sa-NÉ-ri-ou». No «es-ce-NA-rio» con tres.
US: /e/ en NER. UK: /ɑː/ larga, «NAH». El final es el diptongo /oʊ/, «ou», no una o pura.
La s inicial va sin e de apoyo, y la c es /s/, no /θ/ ni /k/: «sa-NÉ-ri-ou».

example.speaker: ryan
example.text: In the worst-case scenario, we go live on June 20.
example.tts: In the worst-case scenario, we go live on June twentieth.

items.meaning: to promise firmly to do something or to meet a date

alerts.text: Acento en MIT; la primera sílaba es schwa: «ka-MIT», no «CO-mit» como *cometer*.
*To* vuelve a ser /tə/: «ka-MIT-ta». La t final de *commit* y la de *to* se funden en una.
Una sola m aunque se escriban dos. Y ojo al significado: *commit to a date* es comprometerse; *compromise* es ceder.

l1.title: A bare future as a forecast
l1.text: Spanish *estará listo el 6* is softened by tone. English *will be ready on the 6th* is a commitment; for a forecast use *should* or *is expected to*.
l1.wrong: The module will be ready on June 6. (meaning: probably)
l1.right: The module should be ready by June 6.

l1.title: Likely as an adverb
l1.text: Spanish *probablemente* tempts *likely* alone before the verb. Use *is likely to* + verb, or *probably*.
l1.right: We're likely to lose another week.

l1.title: Compromise for «compromiso»
l1.text: *A compromise* is an agreement in which both sides give something up. For *comprometerse a una fecha* use *commit to a date*.

l1.title: In the worst of the cases
l1.text: *En el peor de los casos* becomes *in the worst case* or simply *worst case*, not *in the worst of the cases*.
l1.wrong: In the worst of the cases, we go live on the 20th.
l1.right: In the worst case, we go live on the 20th.

l1.title: It's too early, with it
l1.text: Spanish drops the subject (*es pronto para saberlo*). English needs *it*: *it's too early to say*.
l1.wrong: Is too early to say whether the search will be ready.
l1.right: It's too early to say whether the search will be ready.

task.title: Calling a stakeholder back with a date
task.scenario: Helen has asked you, by voice message, for a firm go-live date and the risks to it. Record (or write) your reply: the evidence, a date you can commit to, the date you are aiming for, the main risk and one open point that is too early to decide.
task.brief: Reply to a stakeholder with a graded commitment: evidence → forecast → firm date → risks → next contact.
steps: Thank her and say you have a date.
Give the evidence with *have been + -ing* and *since*.
Commit to one date and name the earlier date you are aiming for.
State the main risk with *unless* or *is likely to*, and one point that is too early to say.
Close with when you will confirm in writing.

chunks.re: \b(should|is likely to|are likely to|'re likely to|is expected to|we expect to|may|realistically|at this stage)\b

extra.title: Extra: the written confirmation
extra.brief: Confirm the same commitment in one formal sentence for Helen's board paper: expected date, the condition, and the point still to be confirmed.

parts.speaker: ryan
parts.text: Hi Helen, {{thanks for your message}}; I have a date for you. {{Since the fix}} last week, we{{'ve been seeing}} far fewer export errors, and the other four modules {{have been running}} without issues for a month, so the reporting module {{should be ready by}} June 6. {{Realistically}}, we{{'re committing to}} June 20 for go-live and {{aiming for}} the 6th. The main risk is the supplier: {{unless}} they change the data format again, the earlier date {{is likely to}} hold. One open point: {{at this stage}} it's {{too early to say whether}} the search will be in the first release; we'll know after Friday's test. {{I'll confirm}} all of this {{in writing by}} tomorrow evening. Thanks!
parts.tts: Hi Helen, thanks for your message; I have a date for you. Since the fix last week, we've been seeing far fewer export errors, and the other four modules have been running without issues for a month, so the reporting module [should](/ʃəd/) be ready by June sixth. Realistically, we're committing to June twentieth for go-live and aiming for the sixth. The main risk is the supplier: unless they change the data format again, the earlier date is likely [to](/tə/) hold. One open point: at this stage it's too early to say whether the search will be in the first release; we'll know after Friday's test. I'll confirm all of this in writing by tomorrow evening. Thanks!
parts.label: Voice reply to the client (neutral, professional)
notes: *Since the fix, we've been seeing… have been running for a month*: two trends as evidence, then *should be ready by*.
*Realistically, we're committing to June 20 and aiming for the 6th*: a firm date and a hope, clearly separated.
*Unless they change the format again, the earlier date is likely to hold*: the risk and its condition in one sentence.
*At this stage it's too early to say whether…*: the open point named, with the date it will be decided.

parts.speaker: emma
parts.text: The reporting module {{is expected to be}} delivered by 20 June, with an earlier release on 6 June {{remaining possible}} {{provided that}} the supplier's data format does not change; the inclusion of the search function {{has yet to be confirmed}}.
parts.tts: The reporting module is expected to be delivered by the twentieth of June, with an earlier release on the sixth of June remaining possible provided that the supplier's data format does not change; the inclusion of the search function has yet to be confirmed.
parts.label: Written confirmation for the board paper (formal)
notes: *Is expected to be delivered by*: the probable date in the passive.
*Remaining possible provided that…*: the earlier date and its condition, in one clause.
*Has yet to be confirmed*: the formal version of *it's too early to say*.
